The serpentine manipulator simulated in the paper has a 13-ft mast, 5 manipulator stages, a wrist, and a gripper end-effector.
The 3 rigid segments in stages 1-3 can bend in the pitch direction from 0-45 degrees.
The flexible couplings in stages 4 and 5 can bend in both pitch and yaw directions, with a pitch range of +/-30 degrees and a yaw range of +/-15 degrees.
The wrist has 2 degrees of freedom: roll (+/-180 degrees) and pitch (+/-60 degrees).
The workspace was discretized into a 21x28 ft. grid with 1 ft. spacing between points.
The evolutionary strategy used a population size of 1 and a mutation operator, with an exponentially decaying annealing factor for the mutation variance.
The authors were able to find inverse kinematic solutions that positioned the end-effector within 1 inch of each target grid point.
The co-evolution process resulted in a solution set with smooth motion, allowing for smooth trajectory generation and following.
The authors' method is the only practically implementable general-purpose approach for determining inverse kinematics in 3D for multi-linked hyper-redundant manipulators.
Prior work on hyper-redundant manipulators relied on simplifying assumptions or was limited to 2D planar manipulators.
The authors had to implement resets and alternate between co-evolving to reduce penalties and improve distances to handle configurations getting 'stuck' during co-evolution.
The authors used bi-linear interpolation of the cell vertex configurations to achieve continuous indexing into the lookup table for inverse kinematics.

The authors incorporated constraints such as joint angle bending restrictions, joint constraints within each stage, and requirements to stay off the hard stops and keep the manipulator above the end-effector.
The authors' approach is applicable for learning the inverse kinematics of a wide variety of hyper-redundant robot designs.
The inverse kinematic solution set obtained using the authors' approach is not unique, but possesses an observable smoothness of motion.
